readerTitle: Why a factory boss handed his workers sledgehammers
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Haier, 1985년 냉장고 파손 일화) + 가상 사례 (불량 비용 단계표, 주방용품 유통 창고)
insight: 품질은 마지막에 검사로 걸러내는 것이 아니라, 실수가 생기는 바로 그 단계에서 만들어진다. 불량은 멀리 갈수록 비싸진다.
misconception: 검사를 늘리면 품질이 올라간다. 품질이 높다는 것은 비싸고 고급스럽다는 뜻이다.

sources.text: Haier Group, company history (1985 refrigerator-smashing story)
Deming, W. E. (1982/1986). Out of the Crisis. MIT Press. (14 Points, Point 3: cease dependence on mass inspection)
National Museum of China collection record of the Haier sledgehammer (news reports, c. 2009)
불량 비용 단계표와 유통 창고 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 1985년 칭다오 냉장고 공장에서 불량 냉장고 76대를 망치로 부순 일화는 Haier 공식 역사에 나옵니다. 숫자 76대, 연도, 장루이민이 첫 망치질을 했다는 세부 내용은 자료마다 조금씩 다를 수 있어 카드에 'As Haier tells the story', 'reportedly'로 표시했습니다. 게시 전 Haier 공식 자료로 다시 확인하세요.
망치가 중국국가박물관에 소장되었다는 내용은 언론 보도 기준입니다. 확인되지 않으면 3번 카드의 해당 문장을 삭제하세요.
Haier가 세계 최대 가전 기업 중 하나로 성장했다는 표현은 일반적 서술로 썼습니다. 구체적인 순위나 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.
7번 카드의 'Haier followed up with stricter rules and checks at each step'은 일반적 서술입니다. 구체적 제도(품질 연동 급여 등)는 출처 확인 전이라 넣지 않았습니다.
Deming 내용은 직접 인용이 아니라 14개 원칙 중 3번(대량 검사 의존을 멈추고 처음부터 품질을 만들어 넣어라)을 풀어 쓴 것입니다.
5번 카드의 단계별 비용($2, $15, $60, $250+)은 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 업계의 '1-10-100 법칙' 같은 특정 배수를 사실로 제시하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why a factory boss handed his workers sledgehammers
body: In 1985, a struggling refrigerator factory in Qingdao, China, found 76 faulty fridges in its stock. Fridges were scarce and expensive. Almost anyone would have bought them.
The factory head, Zhang Ruimin, had them destroyed instead. That factory later grew into Haier, one of the world's biggest appliance makers.

image.label: Workers with sledgehammers beside a row of fridges
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 1980년대 공장 바닥에 흰 냉장고가 일렬로 서 있고, 작업복 입은 직원들이 망치를 들고 서 있음. 한 냉장고 문에 작은 흠집 표시. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You run the factory. What happens to the 76 faulty fridges?
body: Most faults are scratches and dents. Some affect how the fridge works. Customers are waiting, and staff would gladly buy them at a discount.

options.text: Sell them to staff at a discount
options.feedback: You recover money and nothing is wasted. But everyone learns that a faulty fridge still finds a buyer.

options.text: Repair them and sell them at full price
options.feedback: Customers get working fridges and you keep the revenue. But the process that made 76 bad fridges keeps running, and you keep paying to fix its output.

options.text: Destroy them, and trace each fault back to where it was made
options.feedback: You lose the value of 76 fridges at once. In return, everyone sees that a defect has only one exit: being fixed where it starts.

choice.afterReveal: Zhang chose C. The fridges were the smaller problem. The bigger one was a factory that expected defects to be caught later.

cards.title: The fault belonged to whoever made it.
body: As Haier tells the story, Zhang had each fault traced to the workers responsible. Then those workers smashed the fridges, and he reportedly took the first swing. The story has been retold so often that some details may be polished.

But the message reached every worker. A fault isn't the inspector's problem or the customer's problem. It's a problem at the step where it was made. One of the hammers is reportedly kept at China's National Museum.

cards.title: Quality
body: **Quality** means a product or service does what customers reasonably expect, every time. It's about consistency, not luxury.
The key question is where quality comes from. It's built in at each step of the work, not added at the end. Inspection finds defects. It doesn't stop them being made.
The quality pioneer W. Edwards Deming argued this for decades: stop relying on mass inspection, and **build quality into the process** from the start.

image.label: Quality built at each step versus one inspector at the end
image.brief: 두 개의 생산 라인 비교 인포그래픽. 위 라인: 끝에만 돋보기 든 검사원 한 명, 그 앞에 불량품 더미. 아래 라인: 각 작업대마다 작은 체크 표시, 끝에는 깨끗한 완성품. 로고 없음.

cards.title: A defect gets pricier the further it travels.
body: Take one loose fridge door seal. What it costs you depends on where it's found.

breakdown.label: At the workstation
breakdown.detail: The worker refits the seal on the spot

breakdown.label: In the customer's kitchen
breakdown.detail: Service visit, spoiled food, a customer who tells friends

cards.softwareNote: A bug the developer catches takes minutes to fix. The same bug found after release means support tickets, an urgent patch and users who quietly leave.

cards.title: The customer sets the standard, not the price tag.
body: A $10 umbrella that opens every time is high quality for its buyer. A $300 umbrella with a jammed button isn't.

So the first quality question isn't "How good can we make it?" It's "What does the customer **count on**?" For a fridge, it's staying cold and quiet. For a delivery, it's the right item, unbroken, on the promised day.

image.label: Cheap umbrella with a check mark, luxury umbrella with a cross
image.brief: 플랫 일러스트. 왼쪽: 단순한 저가 우산이 활짝 펴져 있고 초록 체크 표시, 가격표 "$10". 오른쪽: 고급 우산이 반쯤 걸려 안 펴지고 빨간 X 표시, 가격표 "$300". 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: The hammer was a signal, not the system.
body: Smashing products only works if the process changes too. Haier followed up with stricter rules and checks at each step. Without that, a dramatic gesture is just an expensive loss.

And more polish isn't always better. Effort spent on details customers never notice is wasted. Put your checks where a fault would hurt customers most, and keep final checks where faults could be dangerous.

cards.title: Now it's a warehouse.
body: You distribute kitchenware to 200 shops. About 3 in every 100 orders arrive with a wrong or missing item, and shops are complaining. Which fix do you choose?

options.text: Add a second person to recheck every box at the packing desk
options.feedback: It will catch many mistakes, but it adds labor to every order and still lets pickers grab the wrong item in the first place.

options.text: Have pickers scan each item at the shelf, so a wrong pick is flagged on the spot
options.feedback: The mistake is stopped where it starts, when it costs seconds to fix. The trade-off is an upfront spend on scanners and setup.

options.text: Send shops an apology credit with every complaint
options.feedback: Shops feel heard, but the errors keep coming and you pay for each one. It's the most expensive defect: the one the customer finds.

cards.title: Catch defects where they're made, not where they're found.
body: Quality is delivering what customers count on, every time. It's cheapest to build in at the step where a mistake begins.
**Try it today:** pick your most common customer complaint. Trace it back to the step where it started. What would it take for that step to catch it?
